# Daily accountability sheet

Who committed to what, by when — a flat commitment log for a daily huddle, honestly flagging anything open past its due date.

Family: Daily management · Format: .xlsx · Domain: core

## What it is

A daily accountability sheet is what a huddle actually checks: specific commitments, each with a real owner and due date. Describe roughly what's been committed to, and specific, checkable commitments get drafted — but status is never guessed. Every commitment starts open, and the sheet flags anything still open once its due date has passed.

## When to use it

Use it when:

- A team runs a daily or near-daily huddle and wants a real record of who owns what, not a verbal list that evaporates by tomorrow.
- You want overdue commitments surfaced automatically, not discovered a week later.
- You want a specific, checkable commitment log, not a vague running list of 'stuff to do.'

Not when:

- The team doesn't actually huddle daily — a sheet nobody checks is worse than no sheet.
- The commitment would just restate an area of ownership ('handle onboarding') rather than a specific, checkable thing.

## How to fill it in

- **commitments** — Drafted from what's been committed to — update real status (open, at-risk, done) yourself as the day goes.
- **narrative** — Drafted from the commitments actually built.

## What good looks like

The example below is the renewal-risk queue's daily sheet, one day after the queue lead's own leader standard work routine. It honestly shows all three real states at once — one commitment done, one overdue, one not yet due — the range a real sheet actually has, not a uniformly tidy list.

Full worked example, on-screen and as a downloadable .xlsx: https://www.katafacts.com/katas/daily-accountability-sheet

## Common mistakes

- **Writing a commitment that's really just an area of ownership restated.** — A real commitment is checkable — 'yes, done' or 'no, not yet' — an area of ownership gives nobody a clear yes or no.
- **Marking something done before it actually is, to keep the sheet looking clean.** — The sheet only has value if it reflects reality — a dishonestly-clean sheet hides exactly the slippage it exists to catch.
- **Letting overdue items sit unaddressed instead of raising them in the huddle.** — The overdue flag exists to trigger a real conversation, not to be a permanent, ignored red mark.

## What it connects to

Upstream:

- **Leader standard work** — Checking the accountability sheet is often literally a leader standard work step — the routine is what makes the sheet get used.

## Where AI helps

Judgement — stays with you:

- Deciding what's genuinely committed versus just discussed
- Deciding how to handle a commitment that's now overdue

Analysis — AI helps:

- Drafting specific, checkable commitments with a real owner and due date from a rough description
- Drafting the narrative from the commitments actually built

Drudgery — automated:

- Tallying done, at-risk, and open commitments
- Identifying which commitments are now overdue
- Exporting to xlsx in the house format
